content:
For offline fundraising in India, the reliable pattern is: print a QR code that opens a dedicated, mobile-friendly landing page on your own NGO website, through a short link tagged with campaign parameters, and then test it on real phones before it goes to the printer. A poster, pamphlet, event banner or receipt that points to your donation or sign-up page can turn footfall into measurable supporters, but only if the code scans, the link opens fast on a patchy connection, and you can later see which poster brought which visitor. This guide covers how to choose between static and dynamic QR codes, how to build a landing page for scanners, how to tag links so Google Analytics 4 can tell you what worked, how to test print sizes, and what to avoid, for any NGO planning NGO website development in India with offline touchpoints in mind.

## Why Offline Fundraising Needs an Online Plan

Many Indian NGOs raise money in person: at community events, school drives, temple and festival stalls, walkathons, hospital corridors and door-to-door campaigns. The donor is standing in front of you with a phone, and the shortest path from interest to action is a scan. Without a plan, three things go wrong:

- The QR code points to the home page, and the donor has to hunt for "Donate".
- The page loads slowly on a weak signal and the donor gives up.
- The NGO cannot tell which event, poster or volunteer produced a gift, so it repeats the weak channels.

A thoughtful setup solves all three. It also pairs well with the work you do online: your [donation page design](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-donation-page-design-2026) is the destination, and your tracking is the feedback.

## Static or Dynamic QR Codes

A QR code stores data (usually a web address) as a pattern of squares. There are two kinds you will meet.

**Static QR codes** contain the destination URL itself. They work forever, need no subscription and no third-party server, but you cannot change where they point after printing. If your URL changes, the printed material is dead.

**Dynamic QR codes** contain a short URL that belongs to a redirect service, which then forwards the scanner to your page. You can change the destination later and often see scan counts. The risks: many services charge subscriptions, and if you stop paying the code may stop working. A code printed on 5,000 pamphlets that dies when a subscription lapses is an expensive mistake.

The most robust choice for an NGO is to run your own redirect on your own domain, for example `yourngo.org/give` or `yourngo.org/q/walk`. The QR code encodes that address; your website forwards it to the current campaign page. You can change the destination without reprinting, nothing depends on a third party's billing, and the printed address is recognisable and trustworthy if someone types it instead of scanning. Your developer can set this up as simple 302 redirects, or as dedicated landing pages. Use a temporary (302) redirect when the destination will change, and a permanent (301) one when it will not.

## Build the Destination First: The Scanner Landing Page

A scanner is on a phone, probably on mobile data, possibly standing in a crowd. Design for that.

### One goal per page
Decide whether the page should collect a donation, a pledge, a volunteer sign-up, an enquiry or a newsletter subscription. A page that offers five options converts fewer people than one that offers one clear action. If you run a donation drive, link straight to a lightweight donation page, not the generic homepage.

### What the page needs, in order
1. A headline that repeats the poster's promise ("Sponsor a child's school kit: Rs 600") so the scanner knows they are in the right place. Use real amounts and real unit costs only; see our guide to [honest unit costs for sponsorship pages](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-sponsorship-programme-pages-sponsor-a-child-meal-2026).
2. One photograph used with consent (see [beneficiary stories and photo consent](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-beneficiary-stories-photos-consent-2026)).
3. A short, tappable amount selector and a primary button.
4. Trust signals visible without scrolling: registration details, tax-exemption information where applicable, and a way to contact a human.
5. A plain statement of what happens to the gift.

### Weight and speed
Keep the landing page small. Compress images, avoid autoplay video, skip heavy pop-ups, and test on a throttled connection. Our guide for [low-bandwidth mobile donors](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-low-bandwidth-mobile-donors-2026) lists practical limits and checks.

### Language
Match the language of the poster. A Marathi pamphlet should open a Marathi page, with an English toggle. See [multilingual donation sites](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-multilingual-hindi-marathi-donation-site-2026).

### No login required
Do not force account creation before a first gift. Offer an account only after the donation, as our guide to [donor accounts and receipts](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-donor-account-giving-history-receipts-2026) suggests.

## Tag Every Link So You Can Tell What Worked

If every QR code points to the same URL, your analytics will lump all scans into "direct" traffic. Instead, give each placement its own tagged link.

Google Analytics 4 reads campaign parameters added to a URL. Google's documentation says that when you add parameters you should always include `utm_source`, `utm_medium` and `utm_campaign`, and strongly recommends also setting `utm_id`. Missing values show up as "(not set)" in reports. An example for a poster at a school event:

`https://yourngo.org/give-school-kit?utm_source=poster&utm_medium=qr&utm_campaign=school_kit_nov2026&utm_content=pune_school_event`

Here:

- `utm_source` is where the code was placed (poster, pamphlet, receipt, banner, volunteer_card).
- `utm_medium` is the kind of channel (qr).
- `utm_campaign` is the campaign (school_kit_nov2026).
- `utm_content` separates variants, such as two locations or two designs (optional).

Keep a single spreadsheet of every tagged link, who created it and where it is deployed. Use lower case, no spaces and consistent names, because GA4 treats "Poster" and "poster" as different values. Our guide to [UTM tracking and campaign naming](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-utm-tracking-campaign-naming-2026) gives a full naming convention.

Then use these tagged URLs as the destination behind your own short link (`yourngo.org/q/school` forwards to the long tagged URL). The QR code encodes only the short address, so it stays simple and scans reliably, while the tagging still happens.

### Check the tracking works
Before printing, scan the code on a phone, make a test donation or form submission, and confirm in GA4's Realtime report that the visit shows the right source and medium and that your key event fires. Our guide to [donation analytics and GA4 funnels](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-donation-analytics-ga4-funnel-2026) explains how to set up the events. Keep the privacy side honest: you are measuring campaign performance, not identifying individual scanners. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs personal data you collect, and your [donor data protection practices](/blog/ngo-donor-data-protection-dpdp-act-2026) should cover analytics and forms.

## Designing a QR Code That Scans

QR codes are standardised in ISO/IEC 18004. A few practical rules prevent the commonest failures.

### Error correction
QR codes include error correction at four levels: L (about 7 percent of the code can be damaged and still read), M (about 15), Q (about 25) and H (about 30). Higher levels allow a logo in the centre or survive scuffs, but they make the pattern denser and harder to scan at small sizes. Level M is a sensible default for printed materials; choose Q or H only if you place a logo or expect wear, and then test.

### Quiet zone and contrast
Leave a clear margin (the quiet zone) around the code; the standard specifies four modules of blank space. Use dark code on a light background with strong contrast. Inverted (light on dark) codes work with some scanners but not all, and coloured codes with low contrast fail often. Do not put the code over a busy photograph.

### Size and distance
There is no universal minimum, and any number you read is a rule of thumb, so test. A reasonable approach: for something held in the hand (a pamphlet or receipt), aim for a code a few centimetres across; for a poster read from a metre or two, much larger; for a banner read from several metres, larger again. A common guideline is that the scanning distance is roughly ten times the code's width, so a code scanned from one metre should be about ten centimetres wide. Verify this with real phones in real lighting rather than trusting the formula.

### Short URLs make simpler codes
The longer the encoded address, the denser the pattern. That is another reason to encode a short link on your own domain rather than a long tagged URL.

### Print quality
Print on matte paper where possible; glossy surfaces create glare under bright lights and outdoor sun. Avoid curves, folds and creases through the code. Never print the code across a fold line on a brochure. Never stretch it unevenly.

### Always add a human-readable address
Under every code, print the short address in plain text ("yourngo.org/give") and a brief instruction ("Scan to donate"). Some people do not have a scanner-capable phone or prefer to type, and the text also helps them recognise a legitimate address.

## Security and Trust: Do Not Let Scammers Use Your Poster

QR codes have a trust problem: a malicious person can paste a sticker over your code, sending donors to a fraudulent payment page. This has happened in public places across the world. To reduce the risk:

- Print the visible short address next to the code so people can check it.
- Use tamper-evident materials or place posters where volunteers can see them.
- Check displayed codes periodically at events.
- Tell donors, on the page and on printed material, which official payment channels you use.
- Do not use link shorteners from unknown providers.

If you hear that a fraudulent code was placed over yours, remove it, record the date, and warn your supporters through your official channels. Report the matter to the platform or authorities as appropriate; in India, cyber-crime reports can be filed through the national portal at cybercrime.gov.in.

## Matching the Code to the Setting

### Posters and banners at events
Place the code at eye level, not near the floor or high above the crowd. Pair it with a stall volunteer who can assist, and a second code or short link for people who cannot scan. Use a separate tagged link per event so you can compare turnouts.

### Pamphlets and door-to-door cards
Keep the call to action single and the code prominent on one side. Add the NGO's name, registration details and a phone number so the recipient can verify you.

### Donation receipts and thank-you letters
A QR code on a receipt that leads to a "give again" or "become a monthly donor" page is a natural follow-up. Our guide to [recurring monthly giving](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-recurring-monthly-giving-2026) explains the destination.

### Walkathons and runs
A bib or volunteer badge can carry a code to the participant's personal fundraising page. See [peer-to-peer fundraising pages](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-peer-to-peer-fundraising-pages-2026) and [event registration pages](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-event-registration-walkathon-fundraising-2026).

### Newspaper and magazine advertisements
Print readers scan from a short distance; make the code reasonably large and put the short address nearby. Use a separate campaign value for each publication and date.

### Vehicles, hoardings and public transport
Scanning from a moving vehicle is unrealistic. Use a short, memorable web address as the main call to action and treat the QR code as secondary.

## A Pre-Print Testing Routine

Never send a QR design to the printer without these checks:

1. Scan the on-screen proof with at least three different phones (an older Android, a recent Android, an iPhone) using the built-in camera app.
2. Print a draft on the actual paper at the actual size and scan it from the intended distance, in the lighting where it will be displayed.
3. Confirm the short link opens the right language page quickly on mobile data, not only Wi-Fi.
4. Confirm the tagged visit appears in GA4 with correct source, medium and campaign.
5. Make a test donation or form submission through the whole flow, including the receipt.
6. Ask someone who has not seen it before to use it without help.

Record the date and who tested. If anything fails, fix it before printing, not after.

## After the Event: Reading the Results

Within a week of an event, review:

- **Visits by campaign and content** in GA4, filtered to your campaign name.
- **Key events** such as donation completed, pledge submitted or volunteer form sent.
- **Conversion rate per placement**, as completed actions divided by visits, interpreted cautiously since scan counts from small events are small.
- **Offline notes**, such as which volunteers were present and the weather, since numbers alone miss context.

Do not draw strong conclusions from tiny samples. If a poster at one stall drew 12 visits and another 4, that is a hint, not proof. Repeat tests across several events before changing your whole approach. If some donors also give by cash or bank transfer after meeting you, record those too using your [offline donations process](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-offline-donations-bank-transfer-cheque-cash-pledges-2026) so that your reporting does not undercount the campaign.

## Common Mistakes

- **QR points to the home page.** Scanners lose interest.
- **Dynamic code from a free trial.** It stops working after the trial.
- **No printed fallback address.** Locked out are those who cannot scan.
- **Untested at print size.** Looks fine on screen, fails on the banner.
- **Same link on every placement.** No learning.
- **Desktop-designed landing page.** Tiny buttons, long forms.
- **Collecting more personal data than needed.** Ask only what the receipt and communication need.
- **Not telling volunteers.** If a donor asks a volunteer about the code and they do not know what it is, trust is lost.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Should an NGO use a static or dynamic QR code?
A static code that encodes a short address on your own domain is the safest. It does not depend on a third-party subscription, and your website can forward the address to the current campaign page whenever you like.

### How do I track which poster brought a donation?
Give each placement its own link with utm_source, utm_medium and utm_campaign parameters, as Google Analytics documentation recommends, then read the campaign report in GA4. Use consistent lower-case names to avoid duplicates.

### How big should a QR code be on a poster?
There is no fixed size. A common rule of thumb is a scanning distance of about ten times the code's width, but you should test your actual print with several phones at the real distance and lighting.

### Can someone replace our QR code with a fake one?
Yes, a sticker can be placed over a printed code. Print the short address beside the code, inspect displayed materials, and tell donors which official channels you use.
